title: How to Think Like a System Designer
subtitle: From one feature to millions of users without breaking
intro: You want to build WhatsApp or YouTube for your interview. Where do you even start drawing?
takeaway: System design is choosing trade-offs so your app stays fast and reliable as it grows.

sections.heading: Everyday analogy: planning a city
sections.body:
Think of an app like a city. A Rate Limiter is the traffic light that stops too many cars at once.

A Distributed Key-Value Store is like many warehouses holding copies of the same goods, so anyone can get them quickly.

A News Feed is the newspaper delivery route that decides what each house gets first.

This city view helps you see the next idea: why we need these parts at all.

sections.heading: Why does this exist? Handling scale you can't ignore
sections.body:
A single server works for 100 users. It fails for 10 million.

That is why we design systems like Twitter's Social Graph and Feed or a Chat System like WhatsApp. They split work across many machines.

For example, a Video Streaming Architecture like YouTube stores one video in many places, so viewers in different cities stream fast without waiting.

But splitting work creates new problems, which is what can go wrong.

sections.heading: What can go wrong? When growth breaks things
sections.body:
More users means more failure points.

- If your Rate Limiter is too strict, real users get blocked
- If your Key-Value Store copies lag, people see old data
- If your Notification System retries too much, it floods phones

Good design means picking what to sacrifice: speed, freshness, or cost. You never get all three perfect.

steps.narration: Millions of users send requests at once.
Rate limiter lets fair traffic through, blocks abuse.
Distributed store keeps copies close to users.
Feed and streaming serve the right data fast.

quiz.q: What does a Rate Limiter do in a system?
options: Controls how many requests a user can make
quiz.why: It protects the system from overload by limiting requests per user or IP.

quiz.q: What fails first if usage grows 100x without a Distributed Key-Value Store?
options: One database gets overloaded and slows everyone
quiz.why: A single store becomes a bottleneck; distributing copies spreads load and keeps reads fast.

quiz.q: Why is a News Feed hard to design for Instagram or Twitter?
options: It must rank and deliver fresh posts to millions instantly
It only needs to store one photo
quiz.why: Feeds must fan-out, rank, and stay fast and fresh at huge scale.
